lessons.title: Being a good worker in a pork abattoir
lessons.html:
Your job and your team

A pork abattoir is a team. The person in the lairage, the stunner, the sticker, the scalding team, the shavers, the eviscerators, the trimmers and the chiller team all depend on each other. If one person is late or careless, the whole line slows down or meat is spoiled.

What a good worker does

  • Arrives on time. The line starts at a set time. Clock in and be dressed and ready before the first pig arrives.
  • Follows instructions. Listen to your supervisor. If you do not understand, ask again. It is better to ask than to guess.
  • Keeps to the rules. Hygiene rules, safety rules and the meat inspector's instructions are not optional.
  • Respects others. Speak politely. No shouting, fighting, swearing or bullying. Respect people of every language, culture and gender.
  • Is honest. Report mistakes, injuries and broken equipment. Never take meat or tools home without permission.

Your rights and duties

As a worker you have rights, for example to a payslip, to leave, to safe working conditions and to fair treatment. You also have duties: to do your work properly, to follow safe work rules, and to take care of your own safety and that of others. Under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993, workers must report unsafe conditions and injuries to their supervisor.

Your contract of employment and the company rules tell you more. Read them or ask someone to explain them to you. If you have a problem at work, speak to your supervisor first. Most companies have a grievance procedure for problems that are not solved.

lessons.title: Communication, numbers and records
lessons.html:
Talking and listening

The abattoir is noisy. Machines, pigs and water make it hard to hear. Good communication keeps people safe.

  • Look at the person you are talking to.
  • Speak clearly and keep it short.
  • Repeat an important instruction back: 'You want me to move the detained carcass to rail 3?'
  • Learn the hand signals your plant uses, for example for stopping the line.
  • Shout a clear warning, such as 'Stop!', if someone is in danger.

Working with numbers

You will use numbers every day:

  • Counting. How many pigs came in from a farmer, how many were slaughtered, how many were condemned.
  • Weights. Carcasses are weighed in kilograms (kg). A side weighs about half of the carcass.
  • Time. Break times, clock-in times and how long a task takes.
  • Money. Your pay is in rand (R). Check your payslip: hours worked, overtime, deductions like UIF.

Example: A farmer sends 60 pigs. 2 are condemned. How many are passed? 60 minus 2 equals 58.

Records

Abattoirs keep records for the law and for the clients: delivery notes, kill sheets, temperature logs, cleaning checklists. When you fill in a record:

  1. Write clearly in pen.
  2. Write the date and time.
  3. Write what you actually saw or did. Never fill in a form before the job is done.
  4. Sign your name.

A false record can lead to unsafe meat reaching people. It is also a serious offence at work.

lessons.title: Health, money and growing your career
lessons.html:
Look after yourself

Slaughter work is physical. You stand for long hours, lift, cut and work in cold and wet places.

  • Eat before your shift and drink water during breaks.
  • Sleep enough. Tired workers cut themselves.
  • Never come to work under the influence of alcohol or drugs. It is dangerous and against the rules.
  • Report any illness like diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or a skin infection before you start work. You may spread germs to the meat.
  • Stretch and change position when you can, to protect your back and hands.

If you feel stressed or have personal problems, ask whether your company has an employee wellness programme, or talk to a clinic or someone you trust.

Managing your money

Make a simple budget each month. Write your pay, then list what you must pay first: food, rent, transport, school fees. Save a small amount each month if you can, even R50. Be careful of loans with high interest. Read every contract before you sign it.

Growing your career

In a pork abattoir you can learn new tasks: from lairage to sticking, from shaving to evisceration, then to trimmer, team leader and supervisor. To grow:

  • Do your current job very well.
  • Ask to learn other stations when there is time.
  • Complete your training and keep your certificates safe.
  • Set a goal, for example: 'In two years I want to be a team leader.'

Key points

  • Be on time, follow instructions, and respect your team.
  • Report mistakes, injuries and unsafe conditions honestly.
  • Repeat important instructions back so you are sure you understood.
  • Fill in records truthfully, only after the work is done.
  • Report illness before work, and never work under the influence.
  • Budget your pay and set goals to grow your career.
